angle: 10 employees with 10 audiences beat one founder with one. What I saw at Ramp
linkedin_post:
10 audiences beat one founder's audience.

That's what I saw at Ramp, and what we do now.

In 2020 and 2021, the people with the real presence at Ramp weren't the founders. A lot of the key content creators were early hires on the team. X was the platform that worked, and there was a lot of Twitter talk from them.

We've taken that lesson into our own company. If I have an audience, that's great. But if 10 people here each have their own independent audience, the reach we get is huge.

It shows up most around fundraise announcements and similar moments over the past couple years. We get the whole team involved in posting their own stories, and we coach people on how to do it well.

It makes a world of difference.

One founder posting is a single channel. A team posting is a distribution network.

Who on your team has an audience you're ignoring?

Slide 2: At Ramp in 2020-2021, early hires carried the presence.
Slide 3: X was the platform that worked there.
Slide 4: It was less about the founder, more about the team.
Slide 5: Big announcements are where team reach shows up most.
Slide 6: We get everyone posting their own unique stories.
Slide 7: We coach people on how to post effectively.
Slide 8: One founder is a channel. A team is a network.

lesson.title: Build reach through your team, not just your founder
takeaways: Independent audiences across 10 people add up to far more reach than one founder's audience.
At Ramp, early hires were often the ones with the strongest presence, not the founders.
Announcements like fundraises land harder when the whole team posts their own stories.
lesson.exercise: Before your next company announcement, ask 5 teammates to each write their own post from their personal angle, and spend 15 minutes coaching each one on it.

angle: The Dreamforce stunt drove fewer demos than the LinkedIn post about it
post_first_line: The Dreamforce stunt lost to its own post.
linkedin_post:
The Dreamforce stunt lost to its own post.

The result surprised me, and it changed how I think about IRL marketing.

A few months back, we ran an in real life stunt at Dreamforce. The social post about it ended up driving more demos booked than the stunt itself, by quite a bit.

Some of these stunts work in person, and we have definitely seen that. Others don't. But doing something a little different, outside the box, is always worth it.

We did the same thing around the Super Bowl, with signs in the background of First Take.

With AI lowering the barrier to entry for content, the more you do IRL and translate to social, the better.

The other thing I like about both of these: they came organically from our team.

The stunt is the raw material. The post is where the reach happens.

What's the last IRL thing you turned into content?
carousel: Slide 1: The Dreamforce stunt lost to its own LinkedIn post.
Slide 2: The social post booked far more demos than the stunt itself.
Slide 3: AI is lowering the barrier to entry for content.
Slide 4: Doing things IRL gives you something AI content can't fake.
Slide 5: Some stunts work in person. Some don't. Do them anyway.
Slide 6: The Super Bowl signs on First Take came from the same instinct.
Slide 7: The best ideas came organically from our own team.
Slide 8: Treat the stunt as raw material and the post as the reach.

lesson.title: Do it IRL, win on social
takeaways: The social post about our Dreamforce stunt drove more demos than the stunt itself.
As AI makes content cheaper to produce, real-world moments stand out more.
Not every stunt works in person, but being a little different is always worth trying.
lesson.exercise: Pick one real-world thing your team is already doing this month (an event, a stunt, an office moment) and plan the post about it before it happens, so you capture the photos and video you need.

angle: The first LinkedIn post to write for any founder: your origin story
post_first_line: Tommy Clark opens with one post for every client.
linkedin_post:
Tommy Clark opens with one post for every client.

It's the one format that keeps winning across all the clients Tommy works with.

The post is the story behind your company. Austin has posted a few versions of it on LinkedIn, one earlier and another just a couple weeks back.

This format is consistently among the best performing post types across client accounts. That's why it's always the starting point.

People want to hear how a company began. It humanizes you, and it's a story only you can tell.

It also hits a few checkboxes at once:

- It works as a milestone announcement, and people like to celebrate you.
- It humanizes you.
- It carries conflict and interesting moments, which almost every founding story has.

The conflict is usually the part founders want to skip. Tommy's point is that it's often the part people remember.

What's the most interesting moment in your founding story?

Conflict and interesting moments in the founding story make it stronger.

angle: The simple monthly update post: one metric, 3 wins, 3 learnings, what's next
post_first_line: Tommy Clark shares a 4-part monthly update post.
linkedin_post:
Tommy Clark shares a 4-part monthly update post.

The structure is simple enough that most founders skip the hard part: the first line.

Tommy says to lead with a growth metric or an exciting thing that happened in the past month. A percentage you grew, a revenue milestone, a big logo you landed, a few key hires. Something that catches attention on the timeline.

The more specific the metric, the better. Tommy pointed out that these posts work well for Austin because Austin is okay sharing specific numbers.

After the hook, the format is:

1. Three key highlights from the past month
2. Three learnings from the past month
3. What's next

Tommy also noted this is a lot easier to execute than an origin story post. There's no narrative through line to build. It's a highlight, a list of wins, what you learned, and what comes next.

What's the one metric you'd lead with?

lesson.title: The Simple Monthly Update Post
takeaways: Open with a specific growth metric or exciting event from the past month to catch attention on the timeline.
Follow the hook with 3 highlights, 3 learnings, and what's next.
This format is easier than an origin story because it has no narrative through line.
lesson.exercise: Write down your single most specific metric or milestone from the past month, then list 3 wins, 3 learnings, and what's next in a draft post.

angle: LinkedIn content has asymmetric upside, but stop asking 'content or outbound' and stack both.
post_first_line: Tens of demos booked per month.
linkedin_post:
Tens of demos booked per month.

That's what good LinkedIn content can do, and it barely takes any time.

Content has asymmetric upside. If you're good at it, it's by far the best-returning thing you can do. It's an order of magnitude of tens-plus demos a month for very little time. That's been our lived experience at Unify.

But that's a standout case, not the baseline.

So stop asking "content or outbound?" That's the wrong question.

When you build a pipeline strategy, it needs to be multichannel. The better question is how you keep stacking wins.

Outreach on LinkedIn is one win. Content on LinkedIn is another.

You don't pick one. You stack them.

Which channel are you underinvesting in right now?

Slide 2: Content has asymmetric upside if you're good at it.
Slide 3: It takes surprisingly little time compared to the return.

Slide 5: Stop asking whether content or outbound is better.

Slide 8: Stack your wins instead of picking a side.

lesson.title: Stack channels instead of choosing one
takeaways: Good LinkedIn content has asymmetric upside: tens-plus demos a month for relatively little time.
That result is a standout case, so don't build a plan that depends on it alone.
A pipeline strategy should be multichannel. Ask how to stack wins, not which channel to pick.
lesson.exercise: List every channel generating pipeline for you today. Mark which ones you're underinvesting in, then add one LinkedIn content habit alongside your existing outbound this week.

angle: AI made posting easy. Here's why that makes your stories the only thing worth posting
post_first_line: Tommy Clark says AI killed the how-to post.
linkedin_post:
Tommy Clark says AI killed the how-to post.

The fix is simpler than most people expect, and it isn't a better prompt.

Anyone can toss a prompt into Claude or ChatGPT and get a pretty okay piece of LinkedIn copy. The barrier to entry has dropped drastically, and the timeline is getting more crowded.

So Tommy's advice is to stand out with content AI can't copy. That means shifting from how-to, value-oriented content to how-I content, with more narrative and more stories.

The rule Tommy uses: pair every single take with a story.

The take can be generated by anyone. The story only comes from what you've actually done.

What story could you attach to your last post?

Slide 2: A pretty okay post now takes one prompt.
Slide 3: The timeline is more crowded than ever.
Slide 4: Generic how-to content is now easy to copy.
Slide 5: Shift from how-to content to how-I content.
Slide 6: Add more narrative and stories to your posts.
Slide 7: Pair every single take with a story.
Slide 8: Your stories are the content AI can't copy.

lesson.title: Pair every take with a story
takeaways: Prompting an AI tool has made the barrier to posting on LinkedIn drop drastically, so the timeline is more crowded.
Standing out means creating content AI can't copy, which means shifting from how-to content to how-I content.
A simple rule: pair every single take with a story.
lesson.exercise: Pick your next three post ideas. For each take, write down one real story from your work that backs it up, then lead the post with that story.
